newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Cargill Brazil says buys Paraguay soybean plants.
newsitem.headline: Cargill Brazil says buys Paraguay soybean plants.

text.p: Cargill Inc has bought two soybean crushing facilities in Paraguay from Brazilian firm Companhia Marangatu for an undisclosed sum, a spokesman at Cargill in Brazil said.
The plants, in Ciudad del Leste, have a joint crushing capacity of 2,300 tonnes per day. Market sources estimate the purchase at $25 million, according to the financial daily Gaceta Mercantil.

Cargill also plans to expand its existing soybean and corn processing plants in Uberlandia in Brazil's Minas Gerais state. "We are making a large investment of $300 million in Brazil," said spokesman Paulo Prestes.

Of this, $200 million will be spent over the next three to four years on expanding the existing crushing facilities in Uberlandia and building a citric acid plant as well as a feed factory, which should both take 18 to 24 months to complete.

The soybean crushing plant will have its capacity expanded to 3,700 tonnes per day from 1,700 tonnes, making it the largest in Brazil, according to Sergio Barroso, director of Cargill's soybean, fertilizer and sugar operation in Brazil.
"It is taking place now, the soybean plant should be ready in time for the next harvest," said Barroso.

Currently, the largest soybean crushers are Santista's plant in Ponta Grossa with a capacity of 3,100 tonnes per day and Incobrasa's plant in Rio Grande with a 3,000 tonnes capacity, said the Brazilian Association of Vegetable Oils Industries.
The corn processing plant will have its capacity expanded to 1,200 tonnes per day from 800 over the next two years, Barroso said.
Cargill also plans to generate energy at the Uberlandia complex although the details of the plan were not yet available.
"There is a great fear of an energy deficit in Brazil," said Prestes, adding that the timing and size of the project depended on the government's energy plan.
Prestes added that Cargill is considering investing in a cocoa plant in Ilheus, Bahia state, as well as a soybean facility there. ((--Joelle Diderich, Sao Paulo newsroom +55 11 248 5417))
